original: Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., in a 1968 speech where he reflects upon the Civil Rights Movement, states, "In the end, we will remember not the words of our enemies but the silence of our friends." As a teacher, I've internalized this message. Every day, all around us, we see the consequences of silence manifest themselves in the form of discrimination, violence, genocide and war. In the classroom, I challenge my students to explore the silences in their own lives through poetry. We work together to fill those spaces, to recognize them, to name them, to understand that they don't have to be sources of shame. In an effort to create a culture within my classroom where students feel safe sharing the intimacies of their own silences, I have four core principles posted on the board that sits in the front of my class, which every student signs at the beginning of the year: read critically, write consciously, speak clearly, tell your truth. And I find myself thinking a lot about that last point, tell your truth. And I realized that if I was going to ask my students to speak up, I was going to have to tell my truth and be honest with them about the times where I failed to do so. So I tell them that growing up, as a kid in a Catholic family in New Orleans, during Lent I was always taught that the most meaningful thing one could do was to give something up, sacrifice something you typically indulge in to prove to God you understand his sanctity. I've given up soda, McDonald's, French fries, French kisses, and everything in between. But one year, I gave up speaking. I figured the most valuable thing I could sacrifice was my own voice, but it was like I hadn't realized that I had given that up a long time ago. I spent so much of my life telling people the things they wanted to hear instead of the things they needed to, told myself I wasn't meant to be anyone's conscience because I still had to figure out being my own, so sometimes I just wouldn't say anything, appeasing ignorance with my silence, unaware that validation doesn't need words to endorse its existence. When Christian was beat up for being gay, I put my hands in my pocket and walked with my head down as if I didn't even notice. I couldn't use my locker for weeks because the bolt on the lock reminded me of the one I had put on my lips when the homeless man on the corner looked at me with eyes up merely searching for an affirmation that he was worth seeing. I was more concerned with touching the screen on my Apple than actually feeding him one. When the woman at the fundraising gala said "I'm so proud of you. It must be so hard teaching those poor, unintelligent kids," I bit my lip, because apparently we needed her money more than my students needed their dignity. We spend so much time listening to the things people are saying that we rarely pay attention to the things they don't. Silence is the residue of fear. It is feeling your flaws gut-wrench guillotine your tongue. It is the air retreating from your chest because it doesn't feel safe in your lungs. Silence is Rwandan genocide. Silence is Katrina. It is what you hear when there aren't enough body bags left. It is the sound after the noose is already tied. It is charring. It is chains. It is privilege. It is pain. There is no time to pick your battles when your battles have already picked you. I will not let silence wrap itself around my indecision. I will tell Christian that he is a lion, a sanctuary of bravery and brilliance. I will ask that homeless man what his name is and how his day was, because sometimes all people want to be is human. I will tell that woman that my students can talk about transcendentalism like their last name was Thoreau, and just because you watched one episode of "The Wire" doesn't mean you know anything about my kids. So this year, instead of giving something up, I will live every day as if there were a microphone tucked under my tongue, a stage on the underside of my inhibition. Because who has to have a soapbox when all you've ever needed is your voice? Thank you.
simplified:
Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. gave a speech in 1968 about the Civil Rights Movement. He said, "In the end, we will remember not the words of our enemies but the silence of our friends." As a teacher, I have taken this message to heart. Every day, we see what happens when people stay quiet. This silence leads to difference, murder, murder, and war. In my class, I encourage my students to think about the silences in their own lives through poetry. We work together to fill those silences. We recognize them, name them, and understand that they do not have to make us feel ashamed. 

 To create a safe space in my class, I have four main rules on the board at the front of the room. Every student signs these at the beginning of the year. The rules are: read critically, write consciously, speak clearly, and tell your truth. I often think about the last point, tell your truth. I realized that if I want my students to speak up, I also need to tell my truth. I must be honest with them about the times I did not speak up. I grew up in a Catholic family in New Orleans. During Lent, I learned that giving something up was very important. It was a way to show God that I understood his glory. I have given up sugar, McDonald's, French fries, French kisses, and more. But one year, I decided to give up speaking. I thought that giving up my voice was the most valuable offer. However, I didn't realize that I had stopped using my voice a long time ago. I spent a lot of my life telling people what they wanted to hear instead of what they needed to hear. I told myself that I wasn't meant to be anyone's guide because I still needed to understand myself. So sometimes, I just stayed quiet. I thought my silence would make things easier, not knowing that trust does not need words to exist. When Christian was attacked for being gay, I put my hands in my pockets and looked down. I acted like I didn't see what happened. I couldn't use my box for weeks. The lock reminded me of the silence I had put on my lips. It reminded me of the homeless man on the corner who looked at me, hoping for a sign that he was worth seeing. I was more worried about touching the screen on my Apple than about feeding him. When the woman at the fundraising party said, "I'm so proud of you. "It must be so hard teaching those poor, idiot kids," I bit my lip. We needed her money more than my students needed their pride. We listen to what people say, but we often ignore what they do not say. Silence comes from fear. It is feeling your faults make you unable to speak. It is the air leaving your chest because it does not feel safe in your throat. Silence is like the Rwandan genocide. Silence is Katrina. It is what you hear when there are not enough body bags. It is the sound after the rope is tied. It is burning. It is chains. It is privilege. It is pain. There is no time to choose your battles when your battles have already chosen you. I will not let silence stop me from making decisions. I will tell Christian that he is brave and smart like a lion. I will ask the homeless man his name and how his day was, because sometimes people just want to feel human. I will tell that woman that my students can discuss transcendentalism like their last name is Thoreau. Just because you watched one event of "The Wire" does not mean you know anything about my kids. So this year, instead of giving something up, I will live every day as if there is a camera under my tongue. I will act as if there is a stage under my fear. Who needs a box when all you need is your voice? Thank you.
